SECTION – TECHNICAL SCIENCES UDC 004.4 Berezhnoy Andrey bachelor's degree, Peter the Great St. Petersburg polytechnic university St. Petersburg, Russia THE EVOLUTION OF ARCHITECTURAL APPROACHES IN THE DESIGN OF HIGH-LOAD INFORMATION SYSTEMS Abstract: This article describes the stages in the evolution of architectural approaches utilized for developing high-load information systems. It explains the transition from monolithic to service-oriented, microservice-based, distributed, and cloud-native systems. The study emphasizes engineering aspects related to achieving scalability and fault tolerance, including the use of containerization, orchestration, and observability tools. It also describes basic reliability patterns commonly. Principles of decentralization, fault isolation, and graceful degradation have been suggested as resilient system design principles. The article confirms that the choice of model is an essential aspect in determining the reliability and efficiency of systems with varying load and high availability requirements. Keywords: architectural approaches, monoliths, service-oriented architecture, microservices, cloud technologies, distributed systems. Бережной Андрей бакалавр, Санкт-Петербургский политехнический университет Петра Великого Санкт-Петербург, Россия ЭВОЛЮЦИЯ АРХИТЕКТУРНЫХ ПОДХОДОВ В ПОСТРОЕНИИ ВЫСОКОНАГРУЖЕННЫХ ИНФОРМАЦИОННЫХ СИСТЕМ Аннотация: В статье рассматриваются этапы эволюции архитектурных подходов, применяемых при проектировании высоконагруженных информационных систем. Анализируется переход от монолитных архитектур к сервисно-ориентированным, микросервисным, распределенным и облачным решениям. Подчеркиваются инженерные аспекты, связанные с реализацией масштабируемости и отказоустойчивости, включая использование контейнеризации, оркестрации и инструментов наблюдаемости. Описаны основные паттерны устойчивости. Также анализируются принципы децентрализации, изоляции сбоев и деградации в качестве основы устойчивой архитектуры. Подтверждается, что выбор модели влияет на надежность и эффективность систем в условиях переменной нагрузки и высокой доступности.

INTRODUCTION In light of uncontrolled data expansion and ever-increasing performance demands, the challenge of creating systems that operate accurately under significant strain has become especially relevant. Today's information systems are required to serve millions of requests per second, offer horizontal scalability, fault tolerance, and less downtime. The evolution of architectural patterns – monolithic to distributed and microservice-based architectures – is a reaction to growing demands of the digital economy, where scalability and reliability of the system are topmost properties. The purpose of this paper is to analyze the development of architectural paradigms for high-load information system development and identify effective practices in scalability and fault tolerance realization. The study covers key stages in the development of architectural patterns, starting from traditional monolithic systems to new concepts such as microservices and serverless architecture. Special attention is drawn to practical considerations, such as architectural patterns, tools, and technologies that support system resilience and flexibility under high loads. MAIN PART. CHARACTERISTICS OF THE MONOLITHIC APPROACH Monolithic architecture has been an underlying paradigm in software system design for many years, particularly when there are limited resources and no distributed infrastructure. A monolith is a pattern of architecture where the functionality of the entire application is written and deployed as a single executable entity [1]. Everything – business logic, data access layer, internal services, and user interface – resides in a single process and talk to each other by way of in-process calls (fig. 1).

Monolithic architecture, despite its technical and operating simplicity, fails to meet today's needs for scalability, fault tolerance, and change delivery flexibility. It can be applied to narrowly defined or quick-term projects, as well as when centralized control over the system is advantageous. In distributed, high-load, and rapidly changing conditions, however, the monolith proves to be a hindrance to scaling and to system evolution [2]. This has fostered a shift away from more monolithic structures, such as service-oriented architecture and microservices, which are ideally suited to both address operational and organizational concerns. SERVICE-ORIENTED ARCHITECTURE AS A TRANSITION FROM MONOLITH TO DISTRIBUTED SOLUTIONS Service-oriented architecture (SOA) was a necessary evolution to overcome the shortcomings of monolithic architectures – i.e., the close coupling of components, limited scalability, and weak fault tolerance [3]. Its emergence in the early 2000s was a radical paradigm shift with emphasis on modularity, reusability, and component independence. SOA is based on loosely coupled, reusable business services, each performing a clearly defined function and exposed through an interface to enable interaction with other services (fig. 2).

Overall, SOA has made important contributions to such principles as scalability of components, reusability, and modularity. Its application is rightly justified in systems that require high level of integration on different platforms and clearly defined business processes. However, application of rigid standards, reliance on centralized control elements (e.g., ESB), and maintenance complexity make this approach not suitable for dynamic and highly evolving systems. These limitations have opened the door for the development of architectural models – namely microservice-based and event-driven ones, offering greater flexibility and fault tolerance. MICROSERVICE ARCHITECTURES In contrast to SOA, which used to retain a centralized message bus (ESB) and relied on heavyweight standards, microservices offer a lighter and more decentralized ISSN 3034-2627

way of developing distributed systems. The essence of microservice architecture lies in splitting the system into numerous small, isolated services, where each service manages a narrowly defined business function [4]. Each service typically has its database (or isolated data domain) and can be independently developed, deployed, and scaled (fig. 3).
Figure 3. Microservice architecture Inter-service communication is accomplished with light protocols – typically REST (HTTP+JSON) or gRPC – while asynchronous use cases rely on message queues and streaming platforms such as Apache Kafka or RabbitMQ. Microservice architecture deployment is inextricably linked with containerization and automation of deployments. Kubernetes and Containers enable services to be packaged into discrete containers and run on distributed infrastructure through orchestration, thereby allowing systems to scale dynamically according to load. Services can be scaled individually and independently, which makes the architecture extremely efficient for distributed and high-load solutions. Microservice architecture possesses a number of distinguishing characteristics that set it apart from more traditional approaches. On the one hand, it offers high flexibility, scalability, and fault tolerance; on the other hand, it requires a carefully designed engineering infrastructure and mature development and operational processes (table 3). Advantages Failure of a single service does not disrupt the entire system. Enables parallel development by independent teams, speeding up delivery. Each service can use different programming languages, frameworks, and databases. Autonomy and continuous updating work seamlessly with CI/CD and DevOps. Challenges Requires robust inter-service communication channels and failure isolation mechanisms. Demands mature DevOps practices and coordination across teams. Increases complexity in integration, monitoring, and consistency across the system. Requires automated testing, versioning, and rollback mechanisms per service. Needs the execution of centralized logging, distributed tracing, and cohesive alerting approaches. No worldwide transactions; intricate logic is required to maintain consistency among services. Load balancing and also service discovery must be merged and also dynamically controlled (e.g., using etcd, Consul). More architectural and operational loads from configuration management, authentication, and security.
Consequently, microservice architecture presents significant potential for building adaptable and extensible systems; nonetheless, its successful implementation requires a strong degree of technological sophistication, automation, and a solid culture of organizational growth. DISTRIBUTED AND CLOUD ARCHITECTURES The advent of universally accessible digital services, data size increases, and the increasing availability demands have led to world-wide dissemination of distributed and cloud architectures that form the core of scalable and fault-resistant information systems. Distributed and cloud architectures derive their operation from the use of multiple computing nodes deployed across a network to execute operations in collaboration, store and compute data, and ensure constant service availability. A distributed architecture implies that the system’s logic and data are physically located on different servers or clusters, which may be geographically dispersed [7]. ISSN 3034-2627

This model enables resilience to individual node failures and allows for more flexible load management (fig. 4).
Figure 4. Distributed architecture diagram Shared characteristics of a distributed system include network-based interactions among components, independently scalable functional units, and coordination of data in the face of bounded synchrony. Theoretical accounts of such systems' behavior are provided by the CAP theorem, stating that it is impossible to achieve Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance at once – one of these properties must be forfeited at all times. For ensuring consistency in distributed systems, consensus protocols such as Paxos and Raft are used. They are building blocks of modern distributed databases (such as CockroachDB, Etcd, TiDB) and configuration management software. Besides these, eventual consistency models are broadly utilized, where data consistency is ultimately achieved over time – a good compromise for the majority of classes of workloads, especially when in an asynchronous or user-facing interface. Practically, distributed architectures are implemented by cloud platforms such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure that provide abstractions for compute resources, storage, messaging queues, databases, and networking interfaces.

Cloud architecture is a design and deployment model for information systems that relies on the utilization of remotely located computing resources [8]. Cloud architecture realizes flexibility, scalability, and fault tolerance through virtualization, automatic load balancing, and abstraction from the physical infrastructure (fig. 5).
Figure 5. Cloud architecture Cloud architecture is structured around a three-tier model of service delivery, with each tier distinguished by varying levels of abstraction and responsibilities between the provider and the user: • IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) – the fundamental tier that offers virtualized computing resources such as virtual machines, storage systems, and networking hardware. The customer must take care of the operating system, applications, and environment configuration. • PaaS (Platform as a Service) – the middle-level, where the cloud provider delivers a pre-configured development environment for software application development, testing, and deployment. The users are offered managed environments such as databases, server-side components, and development tools. • SaaS (Software as a Service) – the top level of abstraction, enabling users to utilize complete software solutions through a web interface or API, without requiring management of the foundational infrastructure or platform. Container orchestration tools (such as Kubernetes) are a critical part of cloud infrastructure with automated scaling, load balancing, self-healing, and straightforward ISSN 3034-2627

deployment. It is augmented by serverless computing and Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), which provides complete abstraction of infrastructure management and automatic scaling on the function level. Cloud and distributed structures allow for horizontal scalability, and resources can be added dynamically when the demand is high without making any changes to the application's architecture. This is particularly important for unpredictable-demand high-load systems such as streaming platforms, international marketplaces, financial transactional systems, and cloud storage systems. At the same time, distributed architectures involve infrastructure and engineering heaviness. It means addressing challenges such as security in distributed systems, time synchronization, network latency and retries, as well as monitoring distributed metrics. Centralized log management systems (ELK, Loki), distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin), and monitoring systems (Prometheus, Thanos) are utilized to enable observability in large-scale, scalable deployments. SCALABILITY AND FAULT TOLERANCE AS FACTORS OF SYSTEM RESILIENCE IN MODERN ARCHITECTURAL MODELS As modern systems evolve from monolithic to microservices, distributed, and cloud-native architectures, scalability and fault tolerance have become central to engineering high-load information systems. These attributes influence a system’s ability to maintain performance during heightened demand, recuperate from minor failures, and enable seamless digital activities. Scalability is achieved through vertical scaling (adding resources to a node) and horizontal scaling (adding nodes). Vertical scaling, present in traditional systems, is limited by physical limits and budget. Horizontal scaling offers greater flexibility, particularly in microservices and cloud environments, yet it complicates data consistency and replication challenges. Current implementations involve load distribution among tiers (DNS, NGINX, Kubernetes Ingress), data partitioning (MongoDB, Cassandra), and replication methods for reliability and increased read capacity.

Fault tolerance guarantees system reliability even in the face of failures, accomplished through replication, automatic failover, and methodologies such as Circuit Breaker, Retry, and Bulkhead. These patterns highlight the significance of graceful degradation and failure isolation in designs based on microservices. Observability technologies such as Prometheus, Grafana, and OpenTelemetry offer visibility and fault detection and are used to base the timely operations safely. Ultimately, scalability and fault tolerance are complementary pillars of good system design, in which they happen through an integration of architecture, infrastructure, and engineering discipline. CONCLUSION The development of design patterns in constructing high-load information systems has seen a transition from closely linked, centralized systems to flexible, modular, and scalable architectures. Although monolithic patterns provided straightforwardness and uniformity, they are progressively being replaced by serviceoriented and microservices architectures that deliver component independence, fault tolerance, and adaptability to change more easily. Cloud. and distributed architectures have given the technology background to horizontal scaling and global availability but also impose new challenges on interaction models, data consistency, and infrastructure administration. For dynamically growing digital services with time-varying workloads, choosing an architectural model and executing it is of crucial significance for the dependability, efficiency, and resilience of an information system.
